goldens.comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/controllers/embed_controller.rb:15 — The public GET enqueues work before validating the embed URL host, so forged requests can flood Sidekiq with cheap jobs.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the embed_controller.rb code, the `best` action first calls `params.require(:embed_url)` to get the embed_url, then checks if a topic exists via `TopicEmbed.topic_id_for_embed(embed_url)`. If no topic exists, it enqueues `Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...)`. However, the `ensure_embeddable` before_filter runs BEFORE the action, which validates that `SiteSetting.embeddable_host` is set and that the request referer host matches the embeddable_host. So the host validation happens in the before_filter, not after the job is enqueued. The finding claims work is enqueued 'before validating the embed URL host', but the before_filter `ensure_embeddable` validates the referer host before the action runs. The actual embed_url host validation happens in TopicRetriever's `invalid_host?` method which checks `SiteSetting.embeddable_host != URI(@embed_url).host`. So while the referer is validated in the controller, the embed_url itself could potentially be for a different host than the embeddable_host, and the job would be enqueued. However, TopicRetriever.retrieve checks `invalid_host?` before `perform_retrieve`, so invalid hosts won't actually do work. The job is enqueued but exits early. This is still a minor issue (unnecessary job creation) but the actual work is protected.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/topic_retriever.rb:27 — The throttle is committed before retrieval succeeds, causing a retry after a transient failure to no-op and be reported as successful.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the code in lib/topic_retriever.rb lines 24-31, the `retrieved_recently?` method uses `setnx` to set a key and then `expire` to set a 60-second TTL. If `setnx` returns true (key was set), it returns false (not retrieved recently), allowing retrieval to proceed. The issue is that the key is set BEFORE `perform_retrieve` is called, not after. If `perform_retrieve` fails (e.g., network error, HTTP failure), the key remains set for 60 seconds, and any retry within that window will return true from `retrieved_recently?`, causing the retrieval to be skipped. This is a real bug - the throttle should be set after successful retrieval, not before, to allow retries on transient failures.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb:35 — One malformed feed item aborts the loop while retries are disabled, permanently starving every later item until the bad entry is removed.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the poll_feed.rb code, the execute method has `sidekiq_options retry: false` and the poll_feed method iterates through `rss.items.each do |i|`. If any item in the loop throws an exception (e.g., malformed content, nil values, encoding issues with `i.content.scrub`), the entire job fails and won't retry. However, the job runs hourly via `recurrence { hourly }`, so it will run again next hour. The finding claims items are 'permanently starved' but they would be retried on the next hourly run. Additionally, if the RSS feed is fixed or the problematic item is removed, subsequent runs would succeed. The issue is real in that one bad item can abort processing of remaining items in that run, but 'permanently starving' is an overstatement since the job runs hourly. Still, the core issue - that one malformed item prevents processing of subsequent items in the same batch - is a real bug in the loop design.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:22 — Feed-controlled markup is stored as raw HTML without sanitization, allowing a compromised feed to persist script-capable content on the Discourse origin.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, in app/models/topic_embed.rb line 22, the code creates posts with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`. In app/models/post.rb, when cook_method is :raw_html, the cook method returns `raw` directly without any processing: `return raw if cook_method == Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`. The content comes from RSS feeds (poll_feed.rb uses `CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)`) or from ruby-readability parsing. While readability limits tags to 'div p code pre h1 h2 h3 b em i strong a img', the RSS feed content in poll_feed.rb doesn't appear to have sanitization applied before being passed to TopicEmbed.import(). The content is stored and rendered as raw HTML. This is a legitimate security concern - if a feed is compromised or contains malicious content, it could inject scripts since the raw HTML is rendered without sanitization.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:15 — Concurrent imports use a check-then-create sequence, so the unique-index collision aborts one import and can terminate the remainder of its feed batch.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the code in app/models/topic_embed.rb, the import method does check if an embed exists with `TopicEmbed.where(embed_url: url).first` and then creates a new one if blank. There's a unique index on embed_url (from the migration). In a concurrent scenario, two processes could both find no existing embed and both try to create one, causing a unique constraint violation. However, this is wrapped in a Transaction block, and the code doesn't have explicit locking. The finding is technically correct - there's a race condition between the check and create. If two concurrent imports for the same URL occur, one will fail with a unique index violation, which would raise an exception and could abort processing of remaining items in a feed batch. This is a real concurrency bug in the check-then-create pattern.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:11 — The protocol-prefix regex accepts hostless URLs such as http://, allowing permanently invalid embed records to be created.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the code in app/models/topic_embed.rb:11, the regex check is `return unless url =~ /^https?\:\/\//`. This regex checks if the URL starts with 'http://' or 'https://'. The regex `^https?\:\/\/` requires 'http' or 'https', followed by '://', but it doesn't require anything after the '://'. So technically 'http://' alone would match this regex. However, looking at the actual usage - the URL comes from RSS feeds (i.link or i.id) or from embed_url parameters. In practice, 'http://' alone is extremely unlikely to be passed. Additionally, even if such a URL were passed, the subsequent code would likely fail when trying to parse it with URI() or when making HTTP requests. The finding is technically correct that the regex would accept 'http://' but this is a very edge case that's unlikely to cause real issues in practice. The regex is meant as a basic sanity check, not comprehensive URL validation.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:37 — The content hash is advanced even when PostRevisor declines or fails to persist the revision, preventing later polls from retrying the missed update.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the code in app/models/topic_embed.rb lines 30-38, when updating an existing embed: the code calls `revisor.revise!()` and then immediately calls `embed.update_column(:content_sha1, content_sha1)` without checking the return value of `revise!`. The PostRevisor's `revise!` method returns false if the revision fails (as seen in lib/post_revisor.rb line 13: 'return false if not should_revise?'). If the revision fails for any reason, the content_sha1 is still updated, which means future polls will think the content is already up-to-date and won't retry the update. This is a real bug where the hash update is not conditional on the revision succeeding.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:64 — Document-relative links and images are left unresolved, so imported content points at the Discourse embed URL instead of the source article.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the absolutize_urls method in app/models/topic_embed.rb lines 52-70, it checks if href/src start_with?('/') to convert relative URLs to absolute. However, document-relative links (like 'hello' or 'images/wat.jpg' without a leading slash) would NOT be caught by this check since they don't start with '/'. The test in the spec shows contents with '/hello' and '/images/wat.jpg' (with leading slashes), which would be handled correctly. But if the source content had truly relative URLs without leading slashes (e.g., 'hello' or '../page'), they would not be converted. The finding claims document-relative links are left unresolved, which is technically accurate - the code only handles root-relative URLs (starting with '/'), not document-relative URLs (no leading slash).

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/topic_retriever.rb:15 — Host-only validation accepts unsupported schemes such as ftp for the configured host, causing fetches that TopicEmbed.import can never store.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at lib/topic_retriever.rb:15, the invalid_host? method checks `SiteSetting.embeddable_host != URI(@embed_url).host`. This only validates that the host matches, not the scheme. However, looking at TopicEmbed.import in app/models/topic_embed.rb:11, there's already a check `return unless url =~ /^https?\:\/\//` that rejects non-http/https URLs. So even if an ftp:// URL passes the host check in TopicRetriever, it would be rejected by TopicEmbed.import. Additionally, TopicEmbed.import_remote uses `open(url).read` which would fail for unsupported schemes. The finding claims this 'causes fetches that TopicEmbed.import can never store' but TopicEmbed.import explicitly handles this by returning nil for non-http/https URLs. This is not a real bug - the code handles this case appropriately.

adjudication_records.issue_text: db/migrate/20131219203905_add_cook_method_to_posts.rb:3 — The default value 1 backfills every existing post as raw_html even though regular is enum value 0, silently reclassifying user content and bypassing normal cooking.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the migration in db/migrate/20131219203905_add_cook_method_to_posts.rb, it adds a column with default value 1. In app/models/post.rb, the cook_methods enum is defined as `Enum.new(:regular, :raw_html)`, which means :regular = 0 and :raw_html = 1. The migration sets default to 1 (raw_html), but the code in post.rb's cook method shows that raw_html posts skip the cooking pipeline and return raw content directly. This means all existing posts would be treated as raw_html and bypass normal cooking. However, looking more carefully at the cook method: `return raw if cook_method == Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]` - this would cause existing posts to return their raw content instead of being properly cooked. This is a real bug - existing posts would have cook_method=1 (raw_html) when they should have cook_method=0 (regular).

adjudication_records.issue_text: db/migrate/20131217174004_create_topic_embeds.rb:3 — force: true drops any pre-existing topic_embeds table before creation, so running this migration against schema drift irreversibly deletes embed mappings.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, db/migrate/20131217174004_create_topic_embeds.rb uses `create_table :topic_embeds, force: true`. The `force: true` option in Rails migrations will drop an existing table before creating a new one. However, this is a new migration file being added (the file didn't exist before), and topic_embeds is a new table being introduced in this feature. In a normal migration workflow, this migration runs once when first deployed. The 'force: true' would only be problematic if: 1) the table already existed from some other source, or 2) the migration is run multiple times. For a brand new table in a new migration, this is actually a common pattern to ensure clean creation. The finding suggests 'schema drift' scenarios, but in standard Rails migration usage, migrations run sequentially once. While using force: true is generally not best practice in production migrations (it's more appropriate for schema.rb regeneration), calling this a bug that 'irreversibly deletes embed mappings' is speculative - the table doesn't exist yet when this migration first runs.

adjudication_records.issue_text: db/migrate/20131223171005_create_top_topics.rb:3 — Adding force: true makes this migration drop any pre-existing top_topics table before creation, destroying ranking data that rollback cannot restore.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows the migration file db/migrate/20131223171005_create_top_topics.rb being modified to add 'force: true' to create_table. The 'force: true' option in Rails migrations causes the table to be dropped if it already exists before creating it. This is a real problem because: 1) In a migration context, if this migration runs and the table already exists (perhaps from a failed previous run or manual creation), it will silently drop all existing data. 2) This makes the migration non-idempotent in a destructive way - running it twice would lose data. 3) The rollback cannot restore data that was in the table before the migration ran. This is a legitimate correctness/data safety issue.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:13 — import` mutates its caller-owned contents string, creating a hidden boundary side effect that can accumulate attribution markup when the value is reused.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, in app/models/topic_embed.rb line 13, the `import` method does `contents << "\n<hr>\n<small>..."` which mutates the `contents` string parameter in place. This is a real issue because: 1) In poll_feed.rb, the `content` variable is passed to `TopicEmbed.import(user, url, i.title, content)` and if the caller reuses that variable or the RSS item is processed multiple times, the attribution markup would accumulate. 2) The mutation happens before any processing, so the caller's string is permanently modified. This is a legitimate code defect - mutating caller-owned parameters is a hidden side effect that can cause bugs when the caller doesn't expect their data to be modified.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:44 — The persistence model also owns remote fetching and readability parsing, tightly coupling database behavior to an external-I/O implementation.

adjudication.rationale: The finding points out that TopicEmbed model has an import_remote method that performs HTTP fetching and readability parsing (using ruby-readability gem). Looking at the diff, line 44-49 shows `def self.import_remote(user, url, opts=nil)` which uses `open(url).read` and `Readability::Document.new()` to fetch and parse remote content. While this is a valid architectural concern about separation of concerns (mixing persistence with I/O operations), this is a design/architecture opinion rather than a bug, security issue, or correctness problem. The code will function correctly. This is a style/design nit about code organization, not a defect that causes incorrect behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb:20 — feed_key` and its Digest dependency are dead code because no path reads the generated key.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff for app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb, I can see the `feed_key` method is defined on lines 20-22, which creates a key using Digest::SHA1. However, examining the entire file, this method is never called anywhere - not in `execute`, not in `poll_feed`, and not anywhere else in the class. The method appears to be dead code that was perhaps intended for caching/throttling but was never implemented. This is a real issue - unused code that adds unnecessary complexity and a dependency on Digest.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/jobs/regular/retrieve_topic.rb:1 — The job loads `email/sender` even though it never references email delivery code.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at app/jobs/regular/retrieve_topic.rb, line 1 shows `require_dependency 'email/sender'`. The job class RetrieveTopic only uses TopicRetriever to retrieve topics and doesn't use any email functionality. This is indeed an unnecessary require that loads code that isn't used. However, this is more of a code cleanliness/optimization issue rather than a bug, security issue, or correctness problem. The code will still function correctly with this unnecessary require. This is essentially a style/cleanup issue rather than a real defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/controllers/embed_controller.rb:15 — Every cache miss enqueues a job before the per-URL throttle, so reloads or request bursts can grow the Sidekiq queue without bound.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the code flow: In embed_controller.rb:15, when topic_id is nil, it enqueues a job via Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...). The throttling logic is in TopicRetriever#retrieved_recently? which uses Redis setnx with a 60-second expiry. However, this throttle is checked INSIDE the job execution (in TopicRetriever#retrieve -> retrieved_recently?), not BEFORE the job is enqueued. So every request that results in a cache miss (no existing topic_id) will enqueue a new Sidekiq job, even if the URL was just requested. The throttle only prevents the actual HTTP fetch from happening multiple times, but the jobs still get queued. This means rapid reloads or request bursts for the same embed_url will create many jobs in the queue, even though most will be no-ops due to the throttle. This is a real resource/queue growth issue.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/topic_retriever.rb:41 — Each distinct missing URL synchronously repolls and reimports the entire feed, multiplying network, parsing, and database work by the feed size.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at lib/topic_retriever.rb:41, the perform_retrieve method checks if feed_polling_enabled and if so calls Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({}). Looking at app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb, the poll_feed method fetches the RSS feed URL, parses it, and iterates through all items calling TopicEmbed.import for each. This means every time a new embed URL is requested that doesn't exist yet, if feed polling is enabled, the entire feed is re-fetched and re-processed. The TopicEmbed.import method does check if an embed already exists and updates it if content changed, but the network fetch and parsing of the entire feed still happens. This is a real performance issue - each missing URL triggers a full feed poll synchronously, which is inefficient when multiple new URLs are requested.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:48 — Reading an unbounded remote response fully into memory before parsing lets a large page exhaust a worker's memory.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at app/models/topic_embed.rb:48, the code is `doc = Readability::Document.new(open(url).read, ...)`. This uses `open(url).read` which fetches the entire remote URL content into memory before passing it to the Readability parser. If a malicious or misconfigured remote server returns an extremely large response, this could exhaust worker memory. This is a real security/resource exhaustion concern - there's no size limit on the response being read into memory. The `open-uri` library's `read` method will load the entire response body into a string.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb:29 — Feed polling materializes the complete unbounded response and processes every item without a cap, allowing a large feed to monopolize worker memory and time.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the poll_feed.rb code, the `poll_feed` method does `rss.items.each do |i|` which iterates over all items in the RSS feed without any limit. However, this is a scheduled job that runs hourly, and RSS feeds typically have a reasonable number of items (usually 10-50). The TopicEmbed.import method also checks if the URL already exists before creating new content. While there's no explicit cap, this is a background job processing RSS feeds which are inherently bounded by practical feed sizes. The finding suggests this could 'monopolize worker memory and time' but RSS feeds are typically small, and the processing per item is minimal. This is more of a theoretical concern about unbounded iteration rather than a concrete bug - it's defensive programming advice rather than identifying an actual defect.
